passages.happening: “Rid yourselves, therefore, of all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander. Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up in your salvation, now that you have tasted that the Lord is good” (verses 1-3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 1 ended with love and the new birth. Chapter 2 begins with what has to go if love is to grow. Peter names five things, and every one of them poisons a community from the inside: malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, slander. Believers who were being slandered by their neighbours were not to slander one another.

Then a picture from the nursery. A newborn baby does not need to be taught to want milk. It cries for it. Peter's readers have been ‘born again’ (1:23). So they should hunger for what makes them grow, as simply and as strongly as a baby hungers for milk. The ‘milk’ is most likely God's word, which Peter has just spoken of, the word that gave them new birth.

‘Grow up in your salvation.’ Salvation is not only a moment in the past. It is a life that grows.

And they have already ‘tasted that the Lord is good’. They know what it is like. That taste is the reason to come back for more.
passages.ot:
Peter's last line comes from a psalm: “Taste and see that the LORD is good; blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him!” (Psalm 34:8). In the psalm ‘the LORD’ is Israel's God. Peter applies it to the Lord Jesus, as the next verse shows: ‘As you come to Him, the living stone’.

He will quote the same psalm again at length in 3:10-12.
passages.asks: Look at the five things Peter names. Ask which one has crept into how you speak about others. Ask what you are hungry for, and whether God's word is on that list. And ask when you last tasted that the Lord is good.

passages.t: Living stones, and a chosen people
passages.happening:
“As you come to Him, the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight, you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (verses 4-5).

Then three passages of Scripture about a stone: the cornerstone laid in Zion, the stone the builders rejected, and the stone people stumble over (verses 6-8). “They stumble because they disobey the word—and to this they were appointed” (verse 8).

“But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
Peter uses the word ‘stone’ five times in a few lines. Christ is ‘the living stone’: people rejected him, but God chose him. And believers, coming to him, become living stones too, built together into a house for God.

The temple in Jerusalem was God's house, the place of priests and sacrifice. Peter says God is now building another house, made of people, with Christ as the cornerstone, the first stone laid, which set the line for the whole building. In this house every believer is a priest. In Israel only the descendants of Aaron served as priests. Peter gives the title to the whole church. Their sacrifices are ‘spiritual’: praise, good deeds, lives given to God. This is the root of what many later called ‘the priesthood of all believers’.

The same stone has two effects. To those who believe, it is precious. To those who refuse, it becomes something they trip over. ‘To this they were appointed’ is a hard line. Peter does not explain it further here, and Christians read it in the light of their views on God's choosing, set out at 1:1-2.

Then the great titles of verse 9. Every one of them was first Israel's. At Sinai God called Israel ‘a kingdom of priests and a holy nation’. Through Isaiah he called them his chosen people, formed to declare his praise. Peter gives these titles to a church of mostly Gentile believers, people who had been cut off from their own towns. They had lost a place. God had given them a people.

Verse 10 takes its words from the prophet Hosea, who gave his children names that meant ‘Not My People’ and ‘No Compassion’, and then heard God promise to call them ‘My people’ again.
passages.ot:
The three stone passages: “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken” (Isaiah 28:16). “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22). And, “to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (Isaiah 8:14). Early Christians already read these three together as words about Jesus. Peter's wording of Isaiah 28:16, ‘will never be put to shame’, differs from the BSB's Old Testament, ‘will never be shaken’, because he usually follows the old Greek translation.

The titles of verse 9 come from Sinai, “And unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6), and from Isaiah: “The people I formed for Myself will declare My praise” (Isaiah 43:21).

And verse 10 comes from Hosea: “I will say to those called ‘Not My People,’ ‘You are My people,’ and they will say, ‘You are my God’” (Hosea 2:23).
passages.hard:
Peter gives Israel's titles to the church. Does that mean God has finished with Israel, or that the church has taken Israel's place?

Peter does not say so, and Christians answer this question in different ways. Here are the main views, each in its holders' terms. These notes do not choose.

Some hold that the church has taken Israel's place as God's people, a view often called replacement theology; much of the church held it for centuries, often in harsh forms, and many churches now reject it. Others hold a milder view they call fulfilment: God's promises to Israel are fulfilled in Christ, and Israel and the church are one people of God in him. Covenant theology stresses one people of God across both Testaments, and many who hold it also expect a future turning of Jewish people to Christ. Dispensational readings hold that God keeps a distinct future for the Jewish people beside the church. A few hold that Jews are in covenant with God through Moses and need not come to faith in Christ; most churches do not teach this. The notes on Romans 9 to 11 set out these views more fully.

Notice who is speaking. Peter is a Jew, using the words of Israel's own Scriptures to welcome Gentiles into blessings God first gave Israel. Paul, writing of his own people, says, “For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).

On every view, contempt for Jews has no ground here. For centuries some Christians used the New Testament to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why.
passages.asks: Ask whether you think of yourself as a priest, someone who brings God's praise and goodness into the places you go. Ask what it means to be part of a house, not a lone stone. And ask whom you know who feels like ‘not a people’, and how God's people could welcome them.

passages.t: Foreigners who do good, and honour the king
passages.happening:
“Beloved, I urge you, as foreigners and exiles, to abstain from the desires of the flesh, which war against your soul. Conduct yourselves with such honor among the Gentiles that, though they slander you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day He visits us” (verses 11-12).

“Submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as the supreme authority, or to governors as those sent by him to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right. For it is God’s will that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish men” (verses 13-15).

“Live in freedom, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil; live as servants of God. Treat everyone with high regard: Love the brotherhood of believers, fear God, honor the king” (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
‘Beloved, I urge you’ opens a long new section of the letter, running to 4:11, about how to live among people who do not share the faith.

‘Foreigners and exiles’ are two words for people living away from home: resident aliens without citizenship, and temporary visitors. Abraham called himself the same among the Hittites. Believers belong to God's people, so they live everywhere as people whose home is elsewhere.

Their neighbours slandered them as ‘evildoers’. Christians would not go to the festivals for the city's gods, avoided temple banquets, and met privately, and rumours spread. Peter's answer is not to argue harder or to hide. It is to do good, visibly and over time, until slander has nothing to hold on to. Some who watched might even come to ‘glorify God on the day He visits us’, an old phrase for God's coming.

Then the authorities. In the eastern empire the emperor was commonly called ‘king’. Governors ruled the provinces and kept order. If Peter wrote in the early 60s, the emperor was Nero. Believers are to respect this order, because God's will is that government should punish wrong and praise right.

But notice verse 17. ‘Treat everyone with high regard.’ ‘Love the brotherhood.’ ‘Fear God.’ ‘Honor the king.’ The king gets honour, the same honour everyone gets. Fear belongs to God alone. Peter will not make the emperor a god, though the empire expected people to.

And ‘live in freedom’. Believers are not slaves of the state or of public opinion. They are servants of God. That freedom is not a cover for doing wrong.
passages.ot:
God told the exiles in Babylon to do good to the city they lived in: “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper” (Jeremiah 29:7).

Proverbs joins fear of God and respect for the king, in that order: “My son, fear the LORD and the king” (Proverbs 24:21).

And Daniel shows the limit. He served a foreign king faithfully, but when the king's law forbade prayer to God, “three times a day he got down on his knees, prayed, and gave thanks to his God, just as he had done before” (Daniel 6:10).
passages.hard:
Does ‘Submit yourselves ... to every human institution’ mean that Christians must obey rulers in everything?

No. Peter himself, when the authorities ordered the apostles to stop preaching, answered, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). In these very verses he gives the emperor honour, not worship, and keeps fear for God alone. The reason he gives for respecting rulers is that their task is to punish wrong and praise right. Respect for that task is not approval of everything a ruler does.

Christians have long held both together: respect for government as part of God's order, and a refusal to obey any command to do wrong or to deny Christ. Paul says the same in Romans 13, and the notes there set it out. These verses belong to no political party, and they give no ruler a claim to a Christian's conscience.
passages.asks: Ask how you answer people who speak against you: by arguing, by hiding, or by doing good. Ask whether you give honour to those in authority while keeping your fear for God. And ask where your freedom has become a cover for something it should not.

passages.t: Slaves, unjust suffering, and Christ's example
passages.happening:
“Servants, submit yourselves to your masters with all respect, not only to those who are good and gentle, but even to those who are unreasonable. For if anyone endures the pain of unjust suffering because he is conscious of God, this is to be commended. How is it to your credit if you are beaten for doing wrong and you endure it? But if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God” (verses 18-20).

“For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps: ‘He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth.’ When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly” (verses 21-23).

“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. ‘By His stripes you are healed.’ For ‘you were like sheep going astray,’ but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
The ‘servants’ here are household slaves. Slavery was built into the economy and the households of the Roman world. Household slaves worked as cooks, cleaners, tutors, stewards and secretaries. How they were treated depended on the master. They had few legal protections and could be beaten. Many of the first Christians were slaves.

Ancient household rules usually spoke only to masters, about how to manage their slaves. Peter speaks to the slaves themselves, as members of the church and as people who answer to God. And he calls a cruel master's treatment what it is: ‘unjust suffering’.

Then he turns at once to Christ. The word for ‘example’ meant a line of letters that a child traced over when learning to write. Christ's way through suffering is the pattern. He did no wrong. He did not answer abuse with abuse or threats. He ‘entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly’: he left judgment to God.

But Christ is more than an example. ‘He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree.’ Believers can follow his steps, but only he could carry their sins. His wounds bring healing. Peter, who once tried to talk Jesus out of the cross, now writes of it in the words of Isaiah 53.

And the last line gathers all believers, slave and free, into one picture: sheep that had wandered, now come home to their Shepherd.
passages.ot:
Peter weaves this passage from Isaiah 53. “He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth” (Isaiah 53:9). “He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). “But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). “We all like sheep have gone astray” (Isaiah 53:6). “Yet He bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12).

The law of Moses set limits on slavery, and punished kidnapping a person with death: “Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession” (Exodus 21:16). And Job saw master and slave as made by the same God: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them?” (Job 31:15).

The Shepherd is Israel's God: “He tends His flock like a shepherd; He gathers the lambs in His arms” (Isaiah 40:11).
passages.hard:
Why does Peter tell slaves to submit instead of condemning slavery? And does this passage ask people who are being abused to stay and bear it?

Peter does not command the end of slavery here, and that should not be softened. He writes to a small, powerless movement in an empire where slavery was everywhere and slave revolts were crushed with great violence.

But within that world he does what ordinary household rules did not. He speaks to slaves as people who answer to God. He calls their unjust treatment unjust. He puts them alongside Christ, and all believers alongside them as sheep of one Shepherd. Elsewhere, on the most common reading of a debated verse, Paul tells slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21). Many readers see in the New Testament the seeds of the truth that would undo slavery: every person bears God's image, and in Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28).

The history of verses like these is painful. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used them to demand obedience from enslaved Africans and to defend slavery as biblical, while they ignored the equality of all in Christ. That was a misuse, and it was wrong. Christians who opposed slavery drew on the same Bible, on human dignity, the exodus and the gospel. The church's record was mixed, and it must be named honestly.

This passage speaks to people with no way out. It is never a reason to tell someone who is being hurt by another person that they must stay and bear it. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask how you respond when someone treats you unjustly, and whether you have left judgment to God or carried it yourself. Ask whether you have let the church's history with these verses be named honestly. And ask what it means for you that Christ bore your sins, and that you have come home to a Shepherd.
